scenario: Today's retrieval track mostly asks one question: how should retrieved content be handed to a model so that it actually helps? DocFS turns long documents into a file system, so an agent lists directories, searches and reads files to find evidence. OpticalRAG renders documents as images and does retrieval and compression on visual tokens. Another group of papers looks at the limits of retrieved results. CLADE finds that when a passage gives only a coarse category, models stop abstaining and start guessing. The Elastic blog post puts the permission check in a fixed step before anything reaches the LLM. On the cost side, FERN brings Text-to-SQL table selection close to LLM-based systems on some benchmarks without calling a generative LLM, and StaRSE uses static vectors that store only signs to reach very low CPU latency.

papers.title: DocFS: File Systems as Agentic Reasoning Environments for Complex Multimodal Document Question Answering
papers.authors: Bingdian Zhang, Zixuan Li, Long Bai, Xiaolong Jin, Jiafeng Guo, Xueqi Cheng
papers.abstract: VLM-based agents solve complex tasks by iteratively interacting with environments, and their effectiveness depends heavily on how the environment exposes information and provides tools for acting on it. However, constructing an effective environment for complex multimodal document question answering remains challenging: documents usually span many pages, with multimodal contents distributed across hierarchical sections and linked by cross-modal associations, while existing methods organize documents into structured representations that address only the information side of the environment and lack tools aligned with the structure, limiting agents' ability to fully exploit it. We observe that file systems naturally combine structure organization with aligned tools: directories and files encode document structure, while file operations provide rich tools to access file contents. Building on this insight, we propose DocFS, a file-system-based agentic framework that reorganizes raw documents as file systems, where directories mirror the section hierarchy and explicit links connect text with figures, tables, and equations. Based on well-established file system tools such as navigation, search, and reading, agents can iteratively explore the document structure, locate relevant evidence, and understand fine-grained local information. Paired with Qwen3.5-Plus, DocFS achieves state-of-the-art performance on MMLongBench-Doc and FinRAGBench-V, outperforming the strongest baselines by 2.9 and 4.3 percentage points, respectively, and is up to 10.3x faster with up to 10.1x fewer tokens than the strongest baseline during reasoning.
papers.summary: When a VLM agent answers questions over long documents that mix text, figures and tables, the hard part is often how the document is laid out for it, not the model. DocFS takes a plain route: it turns the document into a file system, with sections as nested directories and text, figures, tables and equations stored as separate files, plus index files and relation files that record which text goes with which figure. The agent uses only ready-made operations such as listing a directory, keyword search and reading a file. It first locates candidate evidence, then follows the relation files to fill in context, and finally checks the original page. On MMLongBench-Doc its accuracy is 2.9 points above DocLens, the strongest baseline, and mean reasoning time drops from 359.9 to 43.9 seconds. ==A file system already pairs structure with matching tools==, so no custom interface has to be designed for each document layout.

deep_reading.title: DocFS: File Systems as Agentic Reasoning Environments for Complex Multimodal Document Question Answering

papers.title: OpticalRAG: Pixel-Space Compression for Token-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.authors: Senhao Liu, Yuheng Zhang, Chunyu Wei, Yueguo Chen, Xinran Zhang
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is bottlenecked by the token budget of large language models: feeding long documents into the context window is expensive, while aggressive textual compression discards fine-grained information that is irreversibly lost in a one-dimensional token sequence. We argue that this bottleneck is not fundamental to information density but to the choice of compression \\emph{modality}. Modern visual encoders can pack the contents of a rendered text page into roughly a hundred visual tokens with little semantic loss, opening a new compression-fidelity tradeoff that purely textual methods cannot reach. We present \\textbf{OpticalRAG}, a framework that renders documents as page images, encodes them with a frozen vision encoder, and distills the retrieved visual tokens into as few as 16 injected tokens before passing them to the LLM. Two ingredients make this work without expensive cross-modal training: (i) \\emph{Encoder-Bridged Retrieval}, which projects text-query states into the visual feature space of the frozen encoder, through a projection shared with the compressor, to retrieve visual tokens from a text query, with no contrastive training; and (ii) \\emph{Query-Driven Distillation}, a lightweight cross-attention compressor that condenses the retrieved visual tokens into a small set of query-conditioned prefix tokens. On LongBench-v2, BAMBOO, and LooGLE-v2, OpticalRAG achieves the best compression-aware accuracy (CAP) on all three benchmarks while injecting only 16 tokens, and improves the closed-book Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone by 5.17 points on [this http URL](http://longbench-v2.code/) is available at [this https URL](https://github.com/brighterr/OpticalRAG).
papers.summary: To save tokens, RAG systems usually delete words or summarize the text, and the harder they compress, the more detail they lose. OpticalRAG goes the other way: it renders documents as page images, encodes them into visual tokens with a frozen vision encoder, and does both retrieval and compression on those visual tokens. A text query passes through a light projection into the same visual feature space to find relevant content, and a small cross-attention module conditioned on the query squeezes the 256 retrieved visual tokens into 16 for the LLM. On LongBench-v2 it scores 5.17 points above the same base model without retrieval. On another benchmark, compression methods that keep hundreds to thousands of text tokens get higher raw scores, and its strength is reaching close scores with very few tokens.

deep_reading.title: OpticalRAG: Pixel-Space Compression for Token-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation

papers.title: FERN: Cross-Benchmark Table Retrieval for Text-to-SQL with Frozen Retrievers and Learned Ranking
papers.abstract: Text-to-SQL systems over large pooled catalogs must first retrieve the tables a question needs. We compare against the published table recall of RASL, which uses Claude 3.5 models to extract keywords and select tables, on pooled BIRD, Spider, and Fiben catalogs. FERN (Feature-Engineered Ranking with No generative LLM) instead fuses three frozen retrievers into 100 candidates, describes each with up to 120 features, and reorders them with LightGBM rankers fitted once on BIRD's training questions. On Spider, where it was not fitted, its candidate pool alone reaches RASL's published recall at fifteen tables (98.0), and the ranker raises the share of questions with every gold table in the top five (complete@5) from 83.9% to 95.6%. At five tables, FERN's recall is within one point of RASL's on Spider (96.7 vs 97.0) and on BIRD with its evidence hints (96.6 vs 97.5), and 8.2 points below on BIRD without them (89.3). On 121 real BEAVER questions, without BEAVER fitting, its recall at fifteen (82.1) falls between two BEAVER-trained retrievers (80.8, 84.5), but its complete@15 is below both (49.6 vs 54.5 and 62.0). On Fiben, it falls far short at fifteen tables (54.2 vs 69.2, different question sets), although its recall at fifty is numerically close to RASL's question-only retrieval result (80.7 vs 79.4). On BIRD dev with evidence, non-retrieval features raise complete@5 by 7.7 points over retrieval signals alone. On BIRD dev, median latency is 208 ms per question on one A100, without hosted model calls.
papers.summary: In Text-to-SQL over a catalog of hundreds of tables, the first step is finding the tables a question needs, and the popular approach is to let an LLM read the schema and pick. FERN has no generative LLM in its retrieval path: three off-the-shelf retrievers each fetch candidates into one pool, every candidate table gets a large set of features, and a LightGBM ranker trained once on BIRD's training questions orders them. On Spider, which it was never trained on, the share of questions whose needed tables are all in the top five rises from 83.9% to 95.6%, and its recall at five tables is within one point of RASL, which calls Claude. On BIRD, median latency is about 208 ms per question, and no schema has to be sent to an outside service. The weak spots are just as clear: it falls well behind on BIRD without the evidence hints, and further behind on Fiben.

deep_reading.title: FERN: Cross-Benchmark Table Retrieval for Text-to-SQL with Frozen Retrievers and Learned Ranking

papers.title: StaRSE: Compact Russian Sentence Embeddings with a Sign-Coded Static Encoder
papers.authors: Boris Malashenko, Ivan Jarsky, Egor Soldatov, Vladislav Luzhnov, Sviatoslav Stumpf, Vladislav Shmatkov, Viacheslav Shalamov, Andrey Stankevich, Valeria Efimova
papers.abstract: Transformer sentence encoders provide strong retrieval quality, but their inference cost becomes a bottleneck when embeddings must be produced on CPUs or refreshed frequently. We introduce StaRSE, a compact Russian static sentence encoder that removes Transformer inference at deployment time: token directions are stored as sign bits, token norms are stored separately, and sentences are encoded by mean pooling over norm-scaled sign directions. StaRSE is initialized from ruBERT-base, fine-tuned on Russian adjacent-sentence and task-shaped pairs, and post-trained with a contrastive stage that directly optimizes the sign-projected token table. On RuMTEB, StaRSE reaches a task mean of 51.16, 7.98 points above the strongest included static baseline. The packaged model occupies 11.3 MiB and has a mean CPU latency of 0.08 ms per sentence, compared with an estimated 55.7 MiB 16-bit parameter footprint and 1.43 ms mean CPU latency for the closest-quality contextual encoder. Ablations examine adjacent-sentence supervision, token norms, and direct sign-projected post-training.
papers.summary: When embeddings must be computed on CPUs or refreshed often, the inference cost of a Transformer encoder becomes the bottleneck. StaRSE is a static Russian sentence encoder: each token is looked up in a table to get a fixed vector, the sentence vector is the average of those vectors, and no Transformer runs at serving time. For each token, the table stores only the sign of each dimension of its direction, plus one separate length value. In the last training stage the forward pass already goes through this sign-only table, instead of quantizing after training. On RuMTEB it scores only 2.60 points below the closest contextual encoder, the package is just 11.3 MiB, and single-sentence CPU latency is about 18 times lower. There is a cost: on retrieval-heavy tasks, contextual encoders remain clearly stronger.

papers.title: CLADE: Category-Level Answering from Deficient Evidence in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
papers.authors: S M Rayeed, Charles V. Stewart, Yao Ma
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented systems often retrieve passages that are accurate and relevant but state the answer at a coarser level of granularity than the question requires. For example, a question may ask which specific disease a drug treats (familial hyperlipidemia), while the retrieved passage mentions the broader disease family (hyperlipidemia). Prior work on context sufficiency treats such coarse passages simply as insufficient. We argue that they form a distinct case, which we call resolvable insufficiency: text alone cannot settle the fine-grained answer, but the broader category it mentions maps to a short list of candidate answers in a domain ontology. When language models read these coarse, family-only passages, they exhibit a phenomenon we call Clade (Category-Level Answering from Deficient Evidence): they answer instead of abstaining or searching further. On biomedical questions from PrimeKG, family-only passages reduce abstention by 13.8 points compared to uninformative passages, and the resulting guesses are wrong about half the time. A counterfactual test confirms the cause: replacing an exact disease name with its broader family name lowers abstention by 17.4 points compared to deleting the sentence. Simple fixes like confidence filtering, scaling to a larger model, and explicitly instructing the model to abstain cannot resolve Clade, and this replicates on ecological species interactions in GloBI. Finally, we test whether an ontology can turn coarse passages into exact answers. Given the correct family, an ontology list includes the true answer in 98.5% of cases, but string matching finds that family on the page for only 19.8%. Letting the model choose the family raises this to 30.0% and end-to-end recovery from 10.0% to 26.8%. Overall, our results show when language models should stop guessing and consult an ontology, and highlight which steps of that process remain unsolved.
papers.summary: Passages retrieved by RAG are often correct but coarser than the question. A question asks which specific disease a drug treats (familial hyperlipidemia), and the passage only says it treats hyperlipidemia. The authors find that when LLMs read such passages that name only the disease family, they abstain less and start guessing within the family. On biomedical questions from PrimeKG, these passages cut abstention by 13.8 points compared with passages that name neither the disease nor its family, and about half of the extra answers are wrong. Confidence filtering, a larger model and an explicit instruction to abstain all fail to stop it. Expanding the family into a candidate list with a disease ontology puts the true answer in the list 98.5% of the time once the family is right, and the real difficulty is finding that family in the passage. ==A passage that names the right family is not enough to answer the question==.

papers.title: Point-in-Time Encoders for Earnings Calls
papers.abstract: Text encoders turn earnings calls into vectors for search, for language models that answer from retrieved passages, and for forecasting models. A live retriever can use an encoder trained once on all available text, as finance retrievers are, but a backtest needs an encoder that read no text written after the date of each vector. To address this look-ahead bias, from 412,248 calls we train vintages under four pretraining recipes, with yearly cutoffs from 2010 to 2024, and each vintage reads only text dated on or before its cutoff. We then fine-tune each vintage on the question-answer pairs of the calls themselves. The vintages we train on calls alone, with 33.8M parameters, retrieve answers on held-out calls better than the general retrievers we tested in every test quarter. Their vectors also raise by about half the rank correlation between next-day returns and forecasts built from past returns and firm size. When each vintage continues the previous one, a later vintage retrieves better on earlier quarters than the vintage available at the time, and a point-in-time language model that answers from the passages the later vintage retrieves inherits the gain. The 2024 vintage of our families also forecasts earnings surprises better, although the interval of this gain includes zero on calls that no vintage read. It forecasts returns no better, so point-in-time vintages matter most for retrieval and little for forecasts of returns.
papers.summary: In a backtest, if the retrieval encoder has read text written after the test date, future information leaks into the results. The authors train a chain of yearly encoder versions on earnings call transcripts, each reading only text dated before its cutoff year, then fine-tune them contrastively on the calls' analyst question-answer pairs. This 33.8M-parameter model retrieves answers better than every general retriever tested in every test quarter. The key point is that a version that kept training on later years retrieves better on earlier calls than the version available at the time. A control that trains on the same number of tokens without new text shows no such gain, so the gain comes from the later text. When its retrieved passages go to an LLM with the same kind of cutoff, the advantage carries over, while return forecasts barely change. ==Retrievers in a backtest need a time cutoff too==.

papers.title: Fine-grained authorization for Elasticsearch RAG with SpiceDB
papers.abstract: Department filters break the first time Engineering shares one document with Sales, so SpiceDB checks each retrieved chunk against a relationship graph before your Elasticsearch RAG pipeline passes it to the LLM.
papers.summary: Enterprise knowledge-base RAG often starts with a department field as the permission filter, but it breaks once Engineering wants to share one document with Sales, or one executive needs an exception. This Elastic blog post moves permissions into a SpiceDB relationship graph: who belongs to which department and who can view which document are each stored as one relationship, and a permission check asks whether a path exists in the graph. Elasticsearch only retrieves by relevance, and before any retrieved chunk reaches the LLM, SpiceDB checks whether the current user may view it. Sharing or revoking is writing or deleting one relationship, with no reindexing. ==The check must sit in a fixed node the agent cannot route around==, because a prompt injection could persuade the model to skip it. Filtering after retrieval leaves fewer chunks, so the authors suggest retrieving several times more candidates before filtering.

papers.title: Graph Visualizations in Prompts for Knowledge Graph Question Answering
papers.authors: Luiz do Valle Miranda, Andreas L. Opdahl, Grzegorz J. Nalepa
papers.abstract: We study when and how multimodal input improves knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) in large vision--language models. Using a controlled evaluation over 1,500 WebQSP and CWQ questions and six VLMs within a fixed KGQA pipeline, we compare text-only prompting against text-plus-graph visualization at the per-question level and analyze performance changes as a function of reasoning complexity, model size, and image layout. Adding a graph image yields an average gain of 1.85 F1 points, driven by strong precision improvements on low-complexity questions (+4.65 F1). Mixed-effects and regression analyses show that these multimodal gains do not depend strongly on model scale, but are highly sensitive to graph layout: image-only settings sharply degrade performance, hierarchical Graphviz layouts outperform less organized renderings, and decomposing large subgraphs into separated paths yields the largest improvements. Taken together, the results indicate that visual prompting primarily aids KGQA by enhancing prediction precision in low-complexity contexts, provided that visual design respects cognitive and perceptual constraints. To optimize both accuracy and inference efficiency, we argue for adaptive visual prompting policies that selectively append diagrams to small, visually sparse subgraphs with well-structured layouts, avoiding unnecessary visual clutter and token overhead on complex queries. We conclude by relating these findings to a visual notation design theory, outlining how principled diagram encoding can guide future multimodal VLM prompting.
papers.summary: In knowledge graph question answering, if the retrieved triples are written as text and a drawn image of the subgraph is attached too, do VLMs answer better? The authors compare question by question on six VLMs, and adding the image raises F1 by 1.85 points on average. The gain comes mainly from precision and sits on structurally simple questions, while complex ones gain almost nothing. How the graph is drawn matters a lot. On one of the models, giving only the image without the text drops F1 by 9.42 points. A clear hierarchical layout helps, a messy layout shrinks the gain or removes it, and splitting a large subgraph into separate reasoning paths works best. Images also cost extra tokens, so the authors suggest attaching a diagram only for small, sparse subgraphs and always keeping the text triples.

papers.title: Multimodal Abstention That Preserves Acquired Correct Answers
papers.abstract: Adding abstention to a task-adapted multimodal model can discard correct answers, including capabilities acquired during adaptation. We formulate abstention repair as maximizing correct abstention on unanswerable questions under a budget on newly lost correct answers. We propose ReFrain (Regression-Free Abstention), which combines a linear probe on first-token logits, threshold calibration on held-out image clusters, and a deterministic veto that replaces rejected outputs with the displayed "none of the above" option while preserving all other responses. "Regression-free" denotes zero loss on the calibration set at the zero-budget target. All abstention methods in our main comparison start from the same answering-SFT checkpoint; we separately track lost correct answers, repaired errors, and retained SFT gains. On Qwen2.5-VL-3B, ReFrain at zero budget retains all 57 SFT-gained answers with no losses and improves correct abstention by 7.30 percentage points. At a 0.5% calibration budget, it reaches 74.05% correct abstention with 8 losses and retains 55 gains; CLIP-UP EmbLoRA reaches 64.65% with 62 losses, 41 repairs, and 40 retained gains. The same probe at its default threshold loses 298 correct answers. With models and thresholds frozen, confirmation on 228 independent question clusters yields 66.05% correct abstention and no losses at the 0.5% point, exceeding EmbLoRA by 32.72 percentage points. Ordinary refusal SFT achieves higher correct abstention at greater regression cost. Code and reproduction materials: [this https URL](https://github.com/ModeLiberaL/ReFrain).
papers.summary: Adding abstention to an already fine-tuned multimodal model often turns questions it used to answer correctly into abstentions, and net accuracy hides these losses. The authors' example is CLIP-UP EmbLoRA: its net accuracy barely moves, yet underneath it loses 62 originally correct answers and fixes 41 others. ReFrain uses a linear probe on the logits of the first output token to score whether a question can be answered, then sets the threshold on a separate set of images at a point where no correct answer is lost. When the score falls below the threshold, the output is replaced with the abstain option the question already offers, and every other output stays unchanged. This way it loses no correct answer and raises the correct-abstention rate by 7.30 points. ==Evaluating abstention means checking which correct answers were lost, one by one==, and net accuracy alone is not enough.

papers.title: Ontology-Guided Knowledge Graph Construction and Robust Evidence Retrieval for Indian Knowledge Systems
papers.authors: Anand Kaniyaar Sriranga Prasad, Avinash Holenarasipur Nagendra, Mohan Raghavan
papers.abstract: Retrieving evidence from Indian Knowledge Systems is complicated by transliteration variants, ambiguous names, and relations distributed across passages. We present an ontology-guided knowledge graph (KG) pipeline that links typed entities and relations extracted with Qwen3-32B to original textual evidence. Retrieval combines sense-aware grounding, bounded graph traversal, lexical anchors, relationship-vector search, and passage reranking. We evaluate KG alone, single-vector retrieval (SV), and KG unions with SV and Entity Notes on 320 questions from Dhara Bench, matching the per-question candidate count across internal systems under BGE and Qwen rerankers. Standalone KG has the highest Precision@5 under both rerankers and the highest MRR@20 in Counting, Composite, and Multi-hop among the evaluated internal configurations. With Qwen, KG achieves Multi-hop MRR@20 of 0.8722, compared with 0.7622 for the fully reranked KG + SV union. The KG + SV + Entity Notes union instead provides the highest overall Recall@20 (0.5134), compared with 0.4347 for KG. On the 15 Multi-hop questions, Qwen KG achieves complete-evidence MRR@20 of 0.4651 versus 0.3372 for SV, while both full unions complete ten questions within twenty results compared with nine for KG. Gemini 3.7 Flash, evaluated through manually reviewed source mappings, re mains stronger on overall MRR and nDCG, while internal systems have category-specific advantages. All comparisons are descriptive. A separate deployment timing study measures mean retrieval times of 20.374 s for KG and 0.646 s for SV. The findings support selecting KG or its unions according to the required balance of early relevance, evidence completeness, and retrieval cost.
papers.summary: Retrieving evidence from Indian Knowledge Systems texts is hard because one name has several transliterated spellings, names are ambiguous, and relations are spread across several passages. The authors use an LLM to extract entities and relations under an ontology and build a knowledge graph, with every relation linked back to its source passage, and retrieval walks a few bounded steps on the graph before reranking. On 320 questions from Dhara Bench, every system gets the same number of candidates. The graph alone gives the most precise top five results, and on multi-hop questions it also ranks the first relevant result highest. Merging the graph results with single-vector retrieval and other channels recovers more of the evidence. The price is speed: graph retrieval takes about 20 seconds per question on average, single-vector retrieval under 1 second. ==Choosing the graph or the merged results depends on whether top-rank precision or complete evidence matters more==.
